abstract: Candida auris (renamed Candidozyma auris) is a multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen designated as a critical global health threat by the World Health Organization. Since its first clinical identification in 2009, C. auris has spread across six continents, forming distinct genetic clades. Although the clades were initially separated geographically, they now coexist in several regions, raising the possibility that different clades could recombine and produce new variants. In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that C. auris can undergo sexual mating and recombination. We show that haploid clinical isolates of C. auris, taken from different clades, can undergo sexual mating to form diploid cells with a single nucleus and the full genomes of both parents. Diploid cells, in turn, readily produce haploid segregants that contain new combinations of the parental chromosomes. Genome sequencing of haploid segregants revealed many instances of recombination, generating hybrid chromosomes with contributions from both parents. These results show definitively that the apparatus for sexual mating, chromosome segregation, and recombination has been preserved in C. auris clinical strains, presumably by purifying selection. These observations raise the possibility that new C. auris strains with increased drug resistance, virulence, or host range could be generated by these innate capabilities.

summary: Shows that clinical Candida auris isolates from different clades can mate, form diploids, and produce recombinant haploid progeny with hybrid chromosomes.
title: Demonstration of sexual mating and recombination in the fungal pathogen Candida auris.
